texts.0: SP, due to insufficient study of the chart features along the planned route, did not recognize most of the ground points near the flight path. SP mismatched prominent linear features with the chart symbology and reported a wrong point on two consecutive legs, and the IP had to take the aircraft and identify the position himself. Basic aircraft control degraded during the search and altitude exceeded 300 ft from the assigned altitude.
texts.1: SP, due to insufficient study of the chart features along the planned route, failed to recognize confidently the ground points near the flight path. SP identified the required points only after the IP pointed out the reference feature verbally, and the correct position report came at the +/- 300 ft altitude limit while attention stayed inside the cockpit. No IP intervention on the controls was required.
texts.2: SP, due to hesitation in matching chart symbology with the terrain picture, did not recognize confidently all of the ground points near the flight path on the first attempt. SP re-checked the chart, cross-referenced the surrounding features and identified the point without any prompting, holding altitude within 150 to 300 ft of the assigned value during the search. The recognition was completed early enough to keep the leg timing usable.
texts.3: SP recognized confidently most of the ground points near the flight path and reported them accurately as they passed abeam. SP matched chart symbology with the terrain picture without hesitation and kept altitude within +/- 150 ft, airspeed within +/- 10 kt and heading within +/- 5 degrees while doing so. Position awareness was maintained continuously throughout each leg.
texts.4: SP recognized every ground point near the flight path immediately and reported each one with the correct relative position. SP used secondary features to confirm each identification before calling it, and the basic flight parameters showed negligible deviations throughout. Position awareness remained fully current from departure to the last turning point.
texts.marginal: SP recognized the ground points near the flight path within standards, but the identifications relied mainly on the largest and most obvious features and hesitation was evident on the smaller ones. The trend is toward slower recognition when the terrain picture is less distinctive, and SP is expected to broaden the use of secondary chart features so that recognition remains confident in low-contrast terrain.

texts_at.1: SP identified the ground point with altitude at about 275 ft from the assigned value, correcting back to the assigned altitude once the feature was called. The delay traced to chart features studied only in outline before the flight rather than checked in detail against the surrounding terrain. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to study the chart features along the route in more detail during planning so recognition does not cost altitude control.
texts_at.2: SP recognized the ground point after re-checking the chart, holding the altitude excursion to about 210 ft during the search. The hesitation came from matching the chart symbology with the terrain picture only on a second look rather than the first. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to compare symbology and terrain together on the first look so the search does not extend into a second one.
texts_at.3: SP recognized the ground point promptly, holding the altitude excursion to about 95 ft while doing so. The small residual traced to a secondary feature that was checked only after the primary one had already been matched. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to check the secondary feature at the same time as the primary one so no residual altitude drift remains.

texts_above.2: SP matched chart symbology with the terrain picture and identified the ground point with the altitude excursion held to about 200 ft during the search. Checking a secondary feature at the same moment as the primary one would remove even that margin on a low-contrast leg. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to good ground point recognition.
texts_above.3: SP recognized each ground point from the terrain picture without hesitation, holding the altitude excursion to about 100 ft while doing so. The technique is already sound; only the least distinctive terrain would still call for a secondary feature to be checked before calling the point. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to very good terrain-to-chart matching.
texts_above.4: SP recognized every ground point immediately from the terrain picture, with the altitude excursion during the search inside about 30 ft. The only refinement available was to note the secondary feature used for each call for the debrief, since the recognition itself needed nothing further. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to excellent ground point recognition.

texts.0: SP, due to not having internalized the map reading sequence, did not use the right map reading technique and worked from the ground to the map instead of Time - Map - Ground. SP searched the whole chart for whatever feature happened to be visible, lost the running estimate of position and required the IP to intervene and re-establish the navigation picture. Heading wandered beyond 10 degrees from the briefed value during the search.
texts.1: SP, due to not having internalized the map reading sequence, did not apply the Time - Map - Ground technique in the correct order and consulted the chart before checking elapsed time. SP restored the correct sequence only after the IP prompted verbally, and heading was at the +/- 10 degrees limit when the correction started. No control intervention by the IP was needed.
texts.2: SP, due to an unrehearsed cockpit routine, started the map reading cycle from the map rather than from elapsed time on the first two checkpoints. SP recognized the error unprompted, re-established the Time - Map - Ground order and completed the remaining checkpoints correctly, with heading held between 5 and 10 degrees of the briefed value during the reorganization. No prompting or intervention was required.
texts.3: SP used the right map reading technique and worked consistently in the Time - Map - Ground order on every checkpoint. SP checked elapsed time first, narrowed the search area on the chart and then looked out for the expected feature, keeping heading within +/- 5 degrees and altitude within +/- 150 ft throughout. The cycle was completed well before each point passed abeam.
texts.4: SP applied the Time - Map - Ground technique on every checkpoint with a fully established cockpit routine and a fixed chart-to-ground scan pattern. SP anticipated each feature before it became visible and confirmed it in a single glance outside, with negligible deviations in heading, altitude and airspeed. The technique was maintained without degradation over the whole route.
texts.marginal: SP used the Time - Map - Ground technique in the correct order and remained within standards, but the sequence broke down briefly whenever two checkpoints came close together. The trend is toward reverting to a ground-to-map search under time pressure, and SP is expected to keep the elapsed-time step first even on compressed legs so that the technique holds at higher checkpoint density.

texts_at.1: SP restored the Time-Map-Ground order with heading at about 9 degrees from the briefed value before the picture stabilized. The reversal traced to a cockpit routine that had not been rehearsed enough to hold under the first checkpoints of the sortie. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training. SP is expected to rehearse the elapsed-time-first sequence on the ground so it holds from the first checkpoint.
texts_at.2: SP re-established the Time-Map-Ground order with heading held to about 7 degrees of the briefed value during the reorganization. The reversal came from starting the cycle at the map on the first two checkpoints before the routine settled. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to open every checkpoint cycle with the elapsed-time check, even the first two of the sortie.
texts_at.3: SP worked the Time-Map-Ground order on every checkpoint, holding heading to about 3 degrees while completing the cycle. The small residual came from a search area on the chart that was narrowed a moment later than the elapsed time check itself. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to narrow the chart search area in the same instant as the elapsed time check.

texts_above.2: SP worked the map reading cycle in the Time-Map-Ground order on every checkpoint, holding heading to about 6.5 degrees of the briefed value while doing so. Narrowing the chart search area in the same instant as the elapsed time check would tighten that margin further on a compressed leg. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to sound map reading sequence.
texts_above.3: SP checked elapsed time first on every checkpoint, narrowed the chart search and then looked outside for the expected feature, holding heading within about 3 degrees throughout. The technique is already sound; only two checkpoints close together would still call for the sequence to be compressed without being reversed. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to sure-handed Time-Map-Ground technique.
texts_above.4: SP applied the Time-Map-Ground technique on every checkpoint with a fully established routine, holding heading inside about 1 degree throughout. The only refinement available was to log the anticipated feature for the debrief, since the sequence itself needed nothing further. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to exceptional map reading discipline.

error_modes.label: TIMELY RECOGNITION OF DEVIATION AND CORRECTION

texts.0: SP, due to an incomplete comparison between the observed and the expected ground picture, was not able to recognize timely the developing deviation from the turning point and executed no correction. SP continued on the erroneous picture until the IP identified the deviation and took the aircraft to regain the route. The recovery required a heading change well beyond 10 degrees and an altitude excursion beyond 300 ft.
texts.1: SP, due to an incomplete comparison between the observed and the expected ground picture, recognized the deviation from the turning point late and executed the appropriate correction only after the IP pointed it out verbally. The correction was initiated with heading already at the +/- 10 degrees limit from the briefed value and the turning point was reached off the planned geometry. No IP control intervention was required.
texts.2: SP, due to a slow first comparison of the terrain picture against the chart, allowed a deviation from the planned track toward the turning point to develop before detecting it. SP identified the discrepancy unprompted, applied a corrective heading and re-established the correct approach to the turning point with heading between 5 and 10 degrees of the briefed value during the correction. The turning point was crossed on plan.
texts.3: SP recognized timely the developing deviations from the turning points and executed appropriate corrections in every case. SP compared the terrain picture against the chart early on each leg, applied small corrections before the error could grow and held heading within +/- 5 degrees and altitude within +/- 150 ft. Every turning point was crossed on the planned geometry.
texts.4: SP detected the first indication of divergence from the planned track well before the turning point and corrected with minimal control input each time. SP anticipated the effect of the wind on the remaining leg and pre-corrected accordingly, leaving negligible deviations at every turning point. No leg required more than a marginal heading adjustment.
texts.marginal: SP recognized the deviations from the turning points and corrected them within standards, but the detection came consistently in the second half of each leg rather than early. The trend is toward larger corrections than necessary near the turning points, and SP is expected to start the terrain-to-chart comparison earlier on each leg so that the corrections stay small.

texts_at.1: SP re-established the approach to the turning point with heading at about 9 degrees from the briefed value before the correction closed. The late recognition traced to a first comparison of the terrain picture against the chart that was made only as the point grew close. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to compare the terrain picture against the chart earlier on the leg so the deviation is caught before it nears the tolerance.
texts_at.2: SP corrected the developing deviation with heading held to about 7 degrees of the briefed value during the correction. The slow start came from a first terrain-to-chart comparison made later on the leg than the technique calls for. The maneuver was flown to the standard the Training Section requires at this point. SP is expected to make the first terrain-to-chart comparison earlier on each leg, before the turning point is close.
texts_at.3: SP recognized the developing deviation early and applied a small correction, holding heading to about 3 degrees while doing so. The small residual came from a comparison that was accurate but a few seconds later than the earliest point it could have been made. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training. SP is expected to move the first comparison a few seconds earlier so the correction needed shrinks further.

texts_above.2: SP compared the terrain picture against the chart early on the leg and applied a corrective heading before the deviation exceeded about 6.5 degrees. Moving that first comparison earlier still, right after roll-out, would leave an even smaller correction to make. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to solid deviation recognition.
texts_above.3: SP compared the terrain picture against the chart early on every leg and applied small corrections before an error could grow, holding heading within about 3 degrees. The technique is already sound; only the least distinctive legs would still call for a second confirming comparison. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to consistently accurate deviation recognition.
texts_above.4: SP detected the first indication of divergence from the planned track well before each turning point, holding heading deviations inside about 1 degree. The only refinement available was to note the exact range at which each divergence was caught for the debrief, since the recognition itself needed nothing further. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to outstanding anticipation of track divergence.

error_modes.label: ATTENTION DIVISION BETWEEN CHART AND AIRCRAFT STATE

texts.0: SP, due to attention captured by the chart while the aircraft state went unmonitored, kept the head down searching for a single ground point and stopped monitoring the flight parameters. The instrument cross-check lapsed completely, altitude departed by more than 300 ft and airspeed by more than 20 kt, and the IP intervened on the controls to restore the aircraft state. Map reading was suspended until the IP handed the aircraft back.
texts.1: SP, due to attention captured by the chart while the aircraft state went unmonitored, allowed the head-down time on a single ground point to extend well past the time available. SP resumed the cross-check only after the IP called the parameters, with altitude at the +/- 300 ft limit and airspeed at the +/- 20 kt limit at that moment. The correction was completed by SP without control intervention.
texts.2: SP, due to a longer than intended head-down interval on the chart, let the instrument cross-check lapse over one leg. SP recognized the omission unprompted, returned to the scan and corrected an altitude excursion between 150 and 300 ft and an airspeed drift between 10 and 20 kt back to the assigned values. Map reading continued afterwards in short, interleaved glances.
texts.3: SP divided attention correctly between the chart, the outside picture and the flight instruments throughout the navigation. SP kept each head-down interval short and returned to the cross-check between glances, holding altitude within +/- 150 ft, airspeed within +/- 10 kt and heading within +/- 5 degrees. No ground point search was allowed to interrupt the monitoring of the aircraft state.
texts.4: SP maintained a continuous cross-check while map reading, with head-down intervals so short that the flight parameters showed negligible deviations at all times. SP timed the chart glances to the quiet parts of each leg and confirmed the aircraft state after every one of them. Attention division remained effective even during the busiest checkpoints.
texts.marginal: SP divided attention between the chart and the flight instruments within standards, but the head-down intervals lengthened noticeably whenever a ground point was not immediately identified. The trend is toward a degrading cross-check under search workload, and SP is expected to break off the chart search at fixed intervals to reconfirm the aircraft state.

texts_at.1: SP resumed the cross-check with altitude at about 275 ft and airspeed at about 18 kt from the assigned values before both were corrected. The extended head-down interval traced to a single ground point search that ran longer than the scan interval allows. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training. SP is expected to break off the chart search at a fixed interval regardless of whether the point has been found.
texts_at.2: SP returned to the scan and corrected an altitude excursion of about 210 ft and an airspeed drift of about 14 kt back to the assigned values. The longer interval came from a chart glance that ran past the point where the cross-check should have resumed. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to time the chart glance itself, not just the recovery, so the interval does not extend past the plan.
texts_at.3: SP kept the cross-check running with altitude held to about 95 ft and airspeed to about 6 kt of the assigned values throughout a chart glance. The small residual came from a glance that ran a moment past the planned interval on one checkpoint. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to hold the same glance length on every checkpoint, including the busiest one.

texts_above.2: SP kept the instrument cross-check running through the chart search, holding altitude to about 200 ft and airspeed to about 15 kt of the assigned values during the busiest glance. Timing the glance itself, not only the recovery, would tighten that margin further on the next dense leg. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to steady attention division.
texts_above.3: SP divided attention between the chart and the flight instruments on a fixed, short interval, holding altitude within about 95 ft and airspeed within about 6 kt throughout. The technique is already sound; only the busiest checkpoint density would still call for the interval to be trimmed a touch further. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to consistently accurate attention division.
texts_above.4: SP maintained a continuous cross-check while map reading, with altitude and airspeed held inside about 30 ft and 2 kt through every chart glance. The only refinement available was to log the glance intervals used for the debrief, since the division of attention itself needed no correction. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to exemplary attention management.

texts.0: SP, due to task sequencing that concentrated all cockpit workload inside the turn, handled an unfolded and unmarked chart while manoeuvring at the turning point. SP lost the chart orientation completely, was unable to continue the Time - Map - Ground cycle and the IP took the aircraft to stabilize it while the chart was refolded. Altitude and heading exceeded 300 ft and 10 degrees respectively during the episode.
texts.1: SP, due to task sequencing that concentrated all cockpit workload inside the turn, was still folding and orienting the chart when the next leg had already started. SP re-established a usable chart set-up only after the IP prompted, and heading was at the +/- 10 degrees limit when the leg was finally flown correctly. No control intervention by the IP was required.
texts.2: SP, due to a chart folded for the wrong leg, needed additional cockpit time to re-orient the map after the first turning point. SP recognized the problem unprompted, re-folded the chart on the straight portion of the leg rather than in the turn and continued the map reading cycle with altitude held between 150 and 300 ft of the assigned value during the reorganization. The remaining legs were flown with the chart correctly prepared.
texts.3: SP managed the chart efficiently in the cockpit, with the map folded and oriented for the leg in use before each turning point. SP handled the workload on the straight portions of the legs and kept altitude within +/- 150 ft, airspeed within +/- 10 kt and heading within +/- 5 degrees. The map reading cycle was never interrupted by chart handling.
texts.4: SP prepared the chart for every leg in advance and moved through the route without any cockpit handling delay. SP anticipated each turn and completed the chart transition before entering it, leaving negligible deviations in the flight parameters. Cockpit workload remained evenly distributed across the whole sortie.
texts.marginal: SP managed the chart in the cockpit within standards, but the transition to the next leg was consistently completed only just before the turning point. The trend is toward chart handling migrating into the turn as the legs shorten, and SP is expected to complete the chart set-up earlier so that the turning points are flown with no cockpit workload remaining.

texts_at.1: SP re-established a usable chart set-up with altitude at about 270 ft from the assigned value while the fold was corrected. The delay traced to workload sequencing that left the chart transition for the turn itself rather than the straight leg before it. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to move the chart transition onto the straight portion of the leg before the turning point.
texts_at.2: SP re-folded the chart on the straight portion of the leg, holding altitude to about 215 ft of the assigned value during the reorganization. The wrong fold came from preparing the chart for the leg after the current one rather than the one actually flown next. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to confirm which leg comes next before folding the chart for it.
texts_at.3: SP managed the chart efficiently on the straight portion of the leg, holding altitude to about 100 ft of the assigned value while doing so. The small residual came from a fold completed a few seconds later than the earliest point it could have been done. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to start the chart transition a few seconds earlier on each leg.

texts_above.2: SP managed the chart on the straight portion of each leg, holding altitude to about 205 ft of the assigned value while the transition was made. Starting that transition a few seconds earlier still would leave even less for the turning point to absorb. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to dependable chart management.
texts_above.3: SP handled the chart workload on the straight portions of the legs on every occasion, holding altitude within about 100 ft throughout. The technique is already sound; only the shortest legs would still call for the fold to begin a moment sooner. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to well-developed cockpit workload management.
texts_above.4: SP prepared the chart for every leg in advance with no cockpit handling delay, holding altitude inside about 30 ft throughout. The only refinement available was to note the exact preparation timing for the debrief, since the workload distribution itself needed no adjustment. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to exceptional chart workload management.

texts.0: SP, due to an interrupted instrument scan while searching the chart for a ground point, did not maintain the assigned navigation altitude. Altitude departed by more than 300 ft from the assigned value and the trend continued unchecked until the IP intervened on the controls. SP had not recognized the excursion before the intervention.
texts.1: SP, due to an interrupted instrument scan while searching the chart for a ground point, allowed the assigned navigation altitude to drift without detecting the trend. Altitude reached 300 ft from the assigned value and SP initiated the correction only after the IP called it verbally. The recovery was flown by SP without control intervention.
texts.2: SP, due to a longer than intended chart glance, let the aircraft drift off the assigned navigation altitude. SP detected the excursion at approximately 200 ft from the assigned value, returned to the scan and regained the altitude promptly and unprompted. The remaining legs were flown within +/- 150 ft.
texts.3: SP maintained the assigned navigation altitude within +/- 150 ft throughout the map reading task. SP interleaved the chart glances with the instrument cross-check so that any developing trend was caught immediately. Altitude control remained accurate and prompt on every leg.
texts.4: SP held the assigned navigation altitude with negligible deviations for the entire route, including during the checkpoint identifications. SP corrected the smallest trend before it became a deviation and never let the altitude wander during a chart glance. Altitude control was unaffected by the map reading workload.
texts.marginal: SP maintained the assigned navigation altitude within standards, but a consistent low trend developed during each extended chart glance and was corrected only at the end of it. The trend is toward larger excursions as the map reading workload increases, and SP is expected to reconfirm the altimeter at the end of every chart glance so that the drift is caught earlier.

texts_at.1: SP returned to the assigned navigation altitude with the excursion at about 280 ft before the trend was fully arrested. The drift traced to an instrument scan interrupted by a chart search that ran longer than the interval allows. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training. SP is expected to reconfirm the altimeter at a fixed point in every chart glance, however long the search runs.
texts_at.2: SP detected the excursion at about 210 ft from the assigned value and returned to the scan promptly. The drift came from a chart glance that ran a little longer than intended before the altimeter was rechecked. The maneuver was flown to the standard the Training Section requires at this point. SP is expected to reconfirm the altimeter as soon as the ground point is found, rather than after the glance has ended.
texts_at.3: SP held the assigned navigation altitude to within about 95 ft while interleaving chart glances with the instrument cross-check. The small residual came from a glance that ran a moment past the usual interval on one checkpoint. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to hold the same interleave rhythm on the checkpoint that took longer to identify.

texts_above.2: SP interleaved chart glances with the instrument cross-check and caught the developing drift at about 200 ft from the assigned value. Reconfirming the altimeter the instant the ground point is found, rather than after the glance ends, would close that margin further. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to good altitude control while map reading.
texts_above.3: SP maintained the assigned navigation altitude within about 95 ft throughout the map reading task, with the chart glances and the instrument cross-check running on a steady interleave. The technique is already sound; only the checkpoint that took longest to identify still drew the interval out by a moment. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to very good altitude discipline during map reading.
texts_above.4: SP held the assigned navigation altitude with the deviation inside about 30 ft for the entire route, including during every checkpoint identification. The only refinement available was to log the interleave rhythm used for the debrief, since altitude control itself needed no correction. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to excellent altitude control under map reading workload.

texts.0: SP, due to power left unadjusted while attention remained on the chart, did not maintain the briefed navigation airspeed. Airspeed departed by more than 20 kt from the briefed value, the leg timing became unusable and the IP intervened to restore the aircraft state. SP had not detected the deviation before the intervention.
texts.1: SP, due to power left unadjusted while attention remained on the chart, allowed the navigation airspeed to drift from the briefed value. Airspeed reached 20 kt from the briefed value and SP adjusted the power only after the IP called it verbally. No control intervention by the IP was needed and the leg timing was recalculated afterwards.
texts.2: SP, due to a delayed power adjustment during a checkpoint identification, let the navigation airspeed drift from the briefed value. SP detected the deviation at approximately 15 kt, corrected the power unprompted and re-established the briefed airspeed before the leg timing was materially affected. Airspeed remained within +/- 10 kt for the rest of the route.
texts.3: SP maintained the briefed navigation airspeed within +/- 10 kt while carrying out the map reading task. SP adjusted the power promptly whenever a trend appeared and kept the leg timing consistent with the flight plan. Airspeed control was accurate throughout the navigation.
texts.4: SP held the briefed navigation airspeed with negligible deviations for the entire route. SP anticipated the power requirement at each altitude and configuration change so that no correction was needed at the checkpoints. Leg timing matched the flight plan on every leg.
texts.marginal: SP maintained the briefed navigation airspeed within standards, but the airspeed decayed slightly on every leg where a checkpoint identification took longer than expected. The trend is toward accumulating timing error over the route, and SP is expected to include the airspeed indicator in the scan between chart glances so that the power is adjusted before the drift develops.

texts_at.1: SP restored the briefed navigation airspeed with the deviation at about 18 kt before the leg timing was materially affected. The drift traced to power left unadjusted through a checkpoint identification that ran longer than expected. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to include the airspeed indicator in the scan during every checkpoint identification, not only after it.
texts_at.2: SP corrected the power with the airspeed deviation held to about 14 kt before the leg timing was affected. The delay came from a power adjustment left for after the checkpoint rather than made during it. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to adjust power as soon as the checkpoint identification begins, not after it is complete.
texts_at.3: SP maintained the briefed navigation airspeed within about 6 kt while carrying out the map reading task. The small residual came from a power adjustment applied a moment after the airspeed had already begun to move. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to anticipate the power change at the start of the identification rather than reacting once the airspeed has moved.

texts_above.2: SP adjusted power promptly during each checkpoint identification, holding the airspeed deviation to about 15 kt of the briefed value throughout. Anticipating that power change at the start of the identification, rather than partway through it, would tighten the margin further. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to good airspeed control while map reading.
texts_above.3: SP maintained the briefed navigation airspeed within about 6 kt while carrying out the map reading task, adjusting power promptly whenever a trend appeared. The technique is already sound; only the longest checkpoint identifications would still call for the anticipation to begin a moment earlier. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to very good airspeed discipline during map reading.

The only refinement available was to log the power settings used for the debrief, since airspeed control itself needed no correction. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to excellent airspeed management under map reading workload.

texts.1: SP, due to an unmonitored heading indicator while the chart was in use, allowed the briefed heading to drift between checkpoints. error_modes.label: USE OF THE CHART AS THE PRIMARY NAVIGATION REFERENCE

texts.0: SP, due to reliance on the automated navigation solution in place of the chart, did not perform map reading and identified no ground points near the flight path. SP flew the route by following the navigation display alone and could not state the position relative to the terrain when asked, so the IP took over the navigation task. The map reading technique was not demonstrated at any stage of the sortie.
texts.1: SP, due to reliance on the automated navigation solution in place of the chart, used the navigation display as the primary reference and consulted the map only after the IP directed it. SP then identified the ground points correctly, but each identification came after the point had already passed abeam. No IP control intervention was required.
texts.2: SP, due to an early preference for the navigation display, began the route by confirming position from the equipment rather than from the terrain. SP recognized the omission unprompted, reverted to the Time - Map - Ground cycle with the chart as the primary reference and identified the subsequent ground points correctly and before they passed abeam. Basic flight parameters stayed within the limits throughout.
texts.3: SP used the chart as the primary navigation reference and identified the ground points from the terrain picture, treating the on-board equipment only as a cross-check. SP maintained a continuous position estimate independent of the equipment and held altitude within +/- 150 ft, airspeed within +/- 10 kt and heading within +/- 5 degrees. Map reading was demonstrated fully throughout the route.
texts.4: SP navigated entirely by map reading, calling each ground point from the terrain before any confirmation from the on-board equipment. SP used the equipment only to verify what had already been established from the chart, with negligible deviations in the flight parameters. Independent position awareness was maintained without interruption from departure to recovery.
texts.marginal: SP used the chart as the primary navigation reference within standards, but reached for the navigation display first whenever a ground point was not immediately recognized. The trend is toward the equipment replacing the map reading cycle in the harder segments, and SP is expected to complete the Time - Map - Ground cycle before any cross-check with the on-board equipment.

texts_at.1: SP identified the ground points from the terrain picture once the Time-Map-Ground cycle was resumed, though the first checkpoint of the route had already been confirmed from the navigation display instead. The reliance on the equipment traced to an early preference for the display before the chart-based cycle had been established. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to open the route on the chart-based cycle from the very first checkpoint, not only after the display has been consulted.
texts_at.2: SP reverted to the chart as the primary reference after the second checkpoint had been confirmed from the equipment rather than the terrain. The early preference for the display traced to the navigation task not yet being fully established at the start of the route. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. texts_at.3: SP used the chart as the primary reference for the whole route, with the equipment cross-checked once after the third checkpoint out of habit rather than need. The small residual came from a cross-check that added nothing the chart had not already confirmed. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to reserve the equipment cross-check for points where the chart identification is genuinely in doubt.

texts_above.2: SP reverted to the chart as the primary reference immediately after the early preference for the display was recognized, and confirmed every remaining checkpoint from the terrain before any cross-check. Recognizing that preference before the first checkpoint, rather than the second, would remove the lapse entirely. texts_above.3: SP used the chart as the primary navigation reference throughout the route, treating the on-board equipment only as an occasional cross-check. error_modes.label: CHECKPOINT LOOK-AHEAD AND ATTENTION FOCUS DISTANCE

SP started searching for each checkpoint only after it had passed abeam, so the running position estimate was lost over consecutive legs. The IP took the A/C and re-established the navigation picture, with heading already more than 10 degrees off the briefed value and altitude beyond 300 ft from the assigned altitude.
texts.1: SP, due to focusing attention too close to the A/C instead of on points 30 seconds to 1 minute ahead, did not have the checkpoints identified by 1 minute out. SP began the ground search only when the point was nearly abeam and reacted in time only after the IP called the look-ahead verbally. Heading was at the 10 degrees limit from the briefed value when the identification was completed, and no control intervention by the IP was required.
texts.2: SP, due to a late start of the chart-to-ground look-ahead, identified the first checkpoints about 30 seconds out instead of 1 minute out. texts.3: SP looked for the checkpoints 2-5 minutes ahead and had them identified by 1 minute out on every leg. texts_at.1: SP had the checkpoint identified with heading at about 9 degrees from the briefed value by the time the look-ahead window was restored. texts_at.2: SP moved the search back to the 2-5 minute look-ahead band with heading held to about 7 degrees of the briefed value while the scan was reorganized. The late start traced to a look-ahead that began closer to the point than the technique calls for. The maneuver was flown to the standard the Training Section requires at this point. texts_at.3: SP kept the checkpoint look-ahead at 2-5 minutes on every leg, holding heading to about 3 degrees while doing so. texts.0: SP, due to crosschecking the navigation with only references off the nose of the A/C, did not exercise a scan as far as could be seen in each direction. SP disregarded the features abeam and behind the wingline, so a growing offset from the planned track produced no chart-to-ground mismatch and the position could not be resolved. The IP intervened on the controls to regain the route after heading exceeded 10 degrees from the briefed value and altitude departed by more than 300 ft.
texts.1: SP, due to crosschecking with only references off the nose, kept the map reading scan inside a narrow forward sector and did not look abeam. texts.2: SP, due to an initially narrow forward-only crosscheck, missed the abeam features on the first leg and had to hold the checkpoint identification open longer than planned. texts.3: SP exercised a scan that included as far as could be seen in each direction and did not limit the crosscheck to references off the nose. texts.4: SP scanned the full sector on both sides throughout the route and used abeam features as readily as those ahead. texts_at.2: SP widened the scan to include lateral references with heading held to about 7 degrees of the briefed value during the reorganization. texts_at.3: SP scanned as far as could be seen in each direction throughout the route, holding heading to about 3 degrees while doing so. texts_above.3: SP exercised a wide scan on every leg and used lateral landmarks as readily as those ahead, holding heading within about 3 degrees throughout. texts_above.4: SP scanned the full sector on both sides throughout the route and used abeam features as readily as those ahead, holding heading inside about 1 degree throughout. The only refinement available was to note which lateral reference confirmed each fix for the debrief, since the scan itself needed no correction. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to exceptional lateral scan discipline.

texts.0: SP, due to failing to note the relationship of how landmarks are arranged in relation to one another, could not separate two similar small towns ahead and selected the wrong one as the next checkpoint. texts_at.2: SP checked the secondary pattern around the point and confirmed the correct checkpoint, holding altitude to about 210 ft of the assigned value during the hesitation. texts_at.3: SP used the relationship between landmarks to confirm every checkpoint, holding altitude to about 95 ft while doing so. Checking that pattern in the same glance as the primary feature, rather than a moment later, would remove the hesitation entirely. texts_above.3: SP noted the relationship of the landmarks to one another and used it to confirm every checkpoint, holding altitude within about 95 ft throughout. error_modes.label: RELIEF INTERPRETATION: CONTOURS, SPOT ELEVATIONS AND MEF
error_modes.source: technique:8.16 RELIEF (Contour Lines, Spot Elevations, MEF, Gradient Tints)

texts.0: SP, due to not taking the contour interval from the chart legend and not using the Maximum Elevation Figures of the grid squares, misread the closely spaced contour lines of a steep slope as gentle rising ground. SP flew the leg without reference to the spot elevations and to the MEF, which already includes 100 to 199 ft of clearance over the highest known feature, and the terrain clearance became the IP's concern. The IP intervened on the controls to climb the A/C after altitude had departed by more than 300 ft from the assigned navigation altitude.
texts.1: SP, due to reading the relief only from the gradient tints and not from the contour lines and MEF, did not anticipate the rising ground on the leg. SP started the climb to restore the assigned navigation altitude only after the IP called the terrain verbally, with altitude at 300 ft from the assigned value. The correction was flown by SP without control intervention.
texts.2: SP, due to a late crosscheck of the contour spacing and the spot elevations ahead, allowed the A/C to settle as the ground rose along the leg. SP detected the trend unprompted at about 200 ft below the assigned navigation altitude, referred to the MEF of the grid square and regained the altitude promptly. The remaining legs were flown with the relief checked ahead of the A/C.
texts.3: SP read the relief correctly from the contour lines, the spot elevations and the Maximum Elevation Figures and anticipated each change of terrain along the route. SP used the contour interval given in the legend and the gradient tints to confirm the terrain picture, keeping altitude within +/- 150 ft of the assigned navigation altitude. Terrain clearance over every grid square remained comfortably above the MEF.
texts.4: SP interpreted the relief continuously and had the MEF of each grid square and the relevant spot elevations available before entering it. SP used the contour spacing to predict the slope of the terrain ahead and held the assigned navigation altitude with negligible deviations. Terrain awareness required no prompting at any point of the route.
texts.marginal: SP interpreted the relief within standards, but the MEF and the spot elevations were consulted only after the terrain had visibly started to rise. The trend is toward a reactive rather than anticipatory use of the relief information, and SP is expected to read the contour interval and the MEF of the next grid square before entering it so that the altitude is set in advance.

texts_at.1: SP regained the assigned navigation altitude with the excursion at about 275 ft below it before the climb was complete. The late correction traced to the contour spacing and the spot elevations ahead being checked only once the terrain had started to rise. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training. SP is expected to read the contour interval and the spot elevations of the next grid square before entering it, not after the ground has begun to rise.
texts_at.2: SP referred to the MEF of the grid square and regained the altitude promptly, holding the deviation to about 210 ft below the assigned value. The late crosscheck traced to contour spacing and spot elevations that were read only once the ground had begun to rise. The maneuver was flown to the standard the Training Section requires at this point. SP is expected to check the contour spacing and the MEF ahead of every grid square before the terrain change becomes visible.
texts_at.3: SP read the relief correctly from the contour lines, the spot elevations and the MEF, holding altitude within about 95 ft of the assigned value. The small residual came from a crosscheck applied a moment after the terrain had begun to rise rather than before. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to read the relief of the next grid square a little earlier so the altitude is set before, not as, the ground rises.

texts_above.2: SP checked the contour spacing and the spot elevations ahead of the grid square and anticipated the rising terrain, holding altitude to about 205 ft of the assigned value. Checking the MEF of the following grid square at the same moment would extend that anticipation further along the route. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to sound relief interpretation.
texts_above.3: SP read the relief correctly from the contour lines, the spot elevations and the Maximum Elevation Figures and anticipated each change of terrain along the route, holding altitude within about 95 ft throughout. The technique is already sound; only the steepest terrain still calls for the MEF of the next square to be checked a moment sooner. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to precise relief interpretation.
texts_above.4: SP interpreted the relief continuously and had the MEF of each grid square available before entering it, holding altitude inside about 30 ft throughout. The only refinement available was to log the MEF used for each grid square for the debrief, since terrain awareness itself needed no correction. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to outstanding relief interpretation.

error_modes.label: SYMBOL SIZE AND CHART SCALE LIMITATIONS
error_modes.source: technique:8.15 CHARTS (Navigational Charts, Scales, Chart Legend)

texts.0: SP, due to judging the real-world size of the features from the size of their symbols on the 1:500.000 sectional, expected a lookout tower and a minor airfield to be as conspicuous as symbols that cover about half a nautical mile and 4.000 ft to scale. SP did not appreciate that the discrepancies between the real world and its chart representation result from the limitations imposed by scale, with road widths alone exaggerated about 20 times, and rejected the correct checkpoints as non-matching. The position was lost and the IP took the A/C to re-establish the route, with heading more than 10 degrees off the briefed value.
texts.1: SP, due to expecting the ground features to match the exaggerated symbol sizes of the sectional, hesitated to accept a checkpoint that looked far smaller than the chart suggested. SP accepted the correct feature only after the IP verbally explained the scale exaggeration, and heading was at the 10 degrees limit when the identification was completed. No control intervention by the IP was required.
texts.2: SP, due to comparing the apparent size of the ground feature with the size of its chart symbol, delayed the identification of a small airfield shown by an open circle. SP recalled unprompted that the symbol sizes do not conform to true scale while the relative positions of the features remain accurate, confirmed the checkpoint from the distance to a nearby road and continued on plan. Heading was held between 5 and 10 degrees of the briefed value during the delay.
texts.3: SP identified the checkpoints from the relative position of the features rather than from the size of the symbols, allowing for the exaggeration of the sectional symbology. SP used the accurate charted distances between objects to confirm each point and held heading within +/- 5 degrees and altitude within +/- 150 ft. No correct feature was rejected because of its apparent size.
texts.4: SP treated the symbol sizes of the 1:500.000 sectional as conventions and worked entirely from the accurate relative positions and distances between the features. SP identified even the small and low-contrast checkpoints on first sight, with negligible deviations in heading, altitude and airspeed. The scale limitations of the chart never delayed an identification.
texts.marginal: SP allowed for the chart scale limitations within standards, but the first comparison was still made on apparent feature size and only then on the relative position of the objects. The trend is toward hesitation over small checkpoints whose symbols are large on the chart, and SP is expected to lead every identification with the charted distance to the neighbouring features.

texts_at.1: SP confirmed the checkpoint from the distance to a nearby road with heading at about 9 degrees from the briefed value before the identification was complete. The delay traced to the apparent size of the feature being compared with its chart symbol rather than with the accurate relative distances on the chart. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to lead every identification with the charted distance to a neighbouring feature rather than the apparent size of the symbol.
texts_at.2: SP recalled that symbol sizes do not conform to true scale and confirmed the checkpoint, holding heading to about 7 degrees of the briefed value during the delay. The initial hesitation traced to the apparent size of a small airfield being compared with the size of its chart symbol. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to lead with the charted distance between features rather than with the apparent size of the symbol.
texts_at.3: SP identified the checkpoints from the relative position of the features rather than from the size of the symbols, holding heading to about 3 degrees while doing so. The small residual came from a distance check applied a moment after the symbol size had already drawn attention. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to lead with the charted distance in every identification, even the ones with a distinctive symbol.

texts_above.2: SP identified the checkpoint from the relative position of the features rather than the size of the symbols, holding heading to about 6.5 degrees of the briefed value while doing so. Leading with the charted distance from the very first look, rather than after the symbol has drawn attention, would remove the delay entirely. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to competent chart scale interpretation.
texts_above.3: SP identified the checkpoints from the relative position of the features rather than from the size of the symbols, allowing for the exaggeration of the sectional symbology, and held heading within about 3 degrees throughout. The technique is already sound; only the smallest and least distinctive symbols still draw a first glance before the distance check follows. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to notably good chart scale awareness.
texts_above.4: SP treated the symbol sizes of the sectional as conventions and worked entirely from the accurate relative positions and distances between the features, holding heading inside about 1 degree throughout. The only refinement available was to log the distances used to confirm each identification for the debrief, since the technique itself needed nothing further. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to superior chart scale interpretation.
